precepts.text: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, always labouring fervently for you in prayers. I bear him record that he hath a great zeal for you, and them that are in Laodicea, and them in Hierapolis. Colosse, Laodicea, and Hierapolis are all in that same region. Epaphras was putting in serious work.
precepts.point: Epaphras was a self-starter. He did not need someone right there to get the ground running. He heard the truth, believed it, and went and taught it.

note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
Epaphras, the “faithful minister of Christ” the Colossians learned from, comes up again at the end of the letter: “Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.”

“For I bear him record, that he hath a great zeal for you, and them that are in Laodicea, and them in Hierapolis.” On the map you see Colosse, then Laodicea and Hierapolis, all in that same region. Epaphras was one of them, and he carried the work through all three cities.

Epaphras was putting in serious work. He heard the truth, believed it, taught it, and kept labouring fervently in prayer for the congregations he raised up, with great zeal for them. He is the example of the brother who takes the truth and gets the ground running in his own region.

precepts.text: The salutation by the hand of me Paul. The subscript in many Bibles reads: written from Rome to the Colossians by Tychicus and Onesimus. Some people's Bibles may not have that, so it was posted on the screen.
precepts.point: Epaphras was a self-starter. He did not need someone right there to get the ground running. He heard the truth, believed it, and went and taught it.

note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
“The salutation by the hand of me Paul. Remember my bonds. Grace be with you. Amen.” Then the subscript many Bibles carry: “Written from Rome to the Colossians by Tychicus and Onesimus.” Some people’s Bibles may not have that line, so it was put up on the screen for everyone to see.

This epistle was written from Rome, while Paul was under house arrest, which parallels Acts 28, and sent to the church at Colosse by Tychicus and Onesimus. Ephesians, Colossians, Philemon, Philippians, 1 Timothy, Titus and 2 Timothy were written in that same time, which is why they overlap and speak of similar topics and the same people.

Paul never went to Colosse. He wrote to a congregation raised up by Epaphras, and sent the letter by brothers who were themselves of that city.

precepts.text: All my state shall Tychicus declare unto you, with Onesimus, a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. Aristarchus my fellowprisoner saluteth you, and Marcus, sister's son to Barnabas. If Marcus is Barnabas' sister's son, that makes Marcus his nephew, which is John Mark.
precepts.point: Epaphras was a self-starter. He did not need someone right there to get the ground running. He heard the truth, believed it, and went and taught it.

note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
“All my state shall Tychicus declare unto you, who is a beloved brother, and a faithful minister and fellowservant in the Lord.” Tychicus carried the letter. “With Onesimus, a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They shall make known unto you all things which are done here.” Onesimus was one of the Colossians.

“Aristarchus my fellowprisoner saluteth you, and Marcus, sister’s son to Barnabas.” If Marcus is Barnabas’ sister’s son, that makes Marcus his nephew: John Mark.

That is the same John Mark that Paul and Barnabas had their dispute over at the end of Acts 15. Barnabas was sticking up for him because he was his nephew. So these closing names are not filler; they tie the letter to the history of the apostles and the men who carried the work.

precepts.text: If a servant say to his master, I will not do as it pleaseth thee; though afterward he do it, he angereth him that nourisheth him. You are not just angering the master, you are also angering the Lord that nourisheth us.
precepts.point: Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal. They claimed they were the masters; did they do that? No. They lived in the big house while we lived in the outhouse, and we never got the forty acres and the mule. So they showed themselves hypocrites and impostors. The verse ends: knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven.

note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
Colossians 3:22, read in context, says “Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God”. Why? Your master was taking care of your clothes, your raiment, your housing, your food. So why would you disrespect him? Number one, that is your brother. Number two, he is doing this for you: as you do your duties and work, he takes care of you.

Sirach says it: “If a servant say to his master, I will not do as it pleaseth thee; though afterward he do it, he angereth him that nourisheth him.” The master nourishes the servant, and a servant who refuses him angers the one that feeds him.

And you are not just angering the master. You are also angering the Lord that nourisheth us. That is the order Colossians 4:1 completes from the other side: the servant honours the master, and the master gives the servant “that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven.”

precepts.text: Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters according to the flesh, as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart. Colossians, Ephesians, and Philemon were all written during the same period, to the same region.
precepts.point: Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal. They claimed they were the masters; did they do that? No. They lived in the big house while we lived in the outhouse, and we never got the forty acres and the mule. So they showed themselves hypocrites and impostors. The verse ends: knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven.

note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
“Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal”. They said that they were the masters. Did they do that? No. They were living in the big house; we were living in the outhouse, and when we got emancipated, did they ever give us the forty acres and the mule? No. So they are showing that they are hypocrites. They are impostors. They’re the damn devil that the Bible speaks of.

Remember, Colossians, Ephesians and Philemon were all written generally at the same time, to the same region. Ephesians says the same thing Colossians does: “Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as unto Christ; Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart”.

The servants are serving “as unto Christ”, as “the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart.” This is instruction to one people serving under Christ, not a charter for the slave masters of America, and the verse ends by reminding the masters they “also have a Master in heaven.”

note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
To go a little deeper into who these servants are, Jeremiah says: “That every man should let his manservant, and every man his maidservant, being an Hebrew or an Hebrewess, go free; that none should serve himself of them, to wit, of a Jew his brother.”

Being a what? An Hebrew, or an Hebrewess. So these servants are Israelites. And the one they served was “a Jew his brother.”

That is the servant and master of Colossians 3:22 and 4:1: Israelite servants and Israelite masters, brothers. Christianity took a scripture about brethren and cherry-picked it to fit its evil narrative over us.

Not one time does the Lord say we are brethren with the other nations, so those masters are Israelites. If your master still believed in the law of sacrifice but you believed on Christ, you still honored him and treated him with respect.

note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
Paul elaborates on the masters: “Let as many servants as are under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honour, that the name of God and his doctrine be not blasphemed.” The servants are under the yoke, the yoke of bondage. If you had a master who still believed in the law of sacrifice, but you believed on Christ, you still honoured him. He follows sacrifice, but you still treat him with respect.

“And they that have believing masters, let them not despise them, because they are brethren”. Now you have Israelite masters who believe on Christ. Don’t despise a master, your brother, that believes on Christ, because they are brethren.

Not one time has the Lord ever said we are brothers with the other nations. So that is showing you those masters are Israelites. When Colossians 4:1 tells masters to give their servants what is just and equal, it is speaking to Israelite masters over Israelite servants, their brethren.

precepts.why:
Now this makes more sense: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.”

Neither Jew nor Greek we already understand from Colossians 3:11: the Greek-speaking Jews and the Jews. Neither bond nor free: the Israelite servant and the Israelite master. Neither male nor female: the manservant and the maidservant, the Israelite man and the Israelite woman.

“for ye are all one”: we are all one nation, under Christ. That is all it is talking about. So the servants and masters of Colossians 4:1 are one people in Christ, and that is why the master must give the servant what is just and equal.

precepts.why:
More on these servants: “For unto me the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought forth out of the land of Egypt: I am the Lord your God.”

The children of Israel are servants, and they are his servants, the ones he brought out of Egypt. That is who the servants of Colossians are, and why the masters must remember they “also have a Master in heaven”: the servants belong to the Lord.

They changed the narrative and flipped the script, inserting themselves into the scriptures where they are not. Where they are, Leviticus shows it right after: “Both thy bondmen, and thy bondmaids, which thou shalt have, shall be of the heathen that are round about you”, and “they shall be your bondmen for ever”. They were originally our possession, but we sinned against our God and became their possession. Don’t worry: it is going to go back to the way it is supposed to be.

precepts.why:
When we read precept upon precept, in the context of the scriptures, we see how we have been lied to as a people. Paul asks: “Who art thou that judgest another man’s servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth.”

Who are you to judge another man’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls. So our real master is Christ. That is the “Master in heaven” of Colossians 4:1, the one both servants and masters answer to.

And the servant is not left alone: “Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.” There it is. For God is able to make him stand.

precepts.text: When this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea. Now it connects: Asia may not name Colosse in the book of Acts, but the churches of Asia are all right there together.
precepts.point: What thou seest, write in a book, and send it unto the seven churches which are in Asia: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. Laodicea was right there next to Colosse. On the map, Philadelphia and Sardis are all right there by Colosse as well.

note.label: The Colossians & The CHRISTIANS of America

precepts.why:
Paul tells the Colossians, “And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea.” The letters went back and forth between Colosse and Laodicea.

Laodicea is the last of the seven churches in Revelation 1:11: “Ephesus, and unto Smyrna, and unto Pergamos, and unto Thyatira, and unto Sardis, and unto Philadelphia, and unto Laodicea.” And Laodicea was right there next to Colosse.

Now it connects better. Colosse may not be named as one of the churches of Asia in the book of Acts, but when you put the map up, the churches of Asia are all right there together: Laodicea, Philadelphia, Sardis, all right there by Colosse. So when John was told to send what he saw “unto the seven churches which are in Asia”, it was the same region and the same people the epistle to the Colossians was written to.

precepts.text: Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time. Be aware of the time you are in.
precepts.point: Not only the Jews, but many also of other nations, took great indignation, and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man, because Onias had a good report even among the other nations. The king was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead; and being kindled with anger, he took away Andronicus his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city unto that very place where he had committed impiety against Onias, and there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.

note.label: From Brother To Betrayer

precepts.why:
“Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time.” Walk in wisdom toward them that are without the truth, that don't know the truth.

“Redeeming the time” means be aware of the time you are in.

It goes with the good report of Onias. He had a good report among the Jews and among the other nations without joining himself to the other nations, and when he was unjustly murdered, the Jews and “certain of the Greeks that abhorred the fact also” complained because he “was slain without cause.” That is walking in wisdom toward them that are without: keeping yourself apart from their ways, and still carrying yourself so that they know you are righteous.

precepts.text: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, always labouring fervently for you in prayers; for I bear him record, that he hath a great zeal for you, and them that are in Laodicea, and them in Hierapolis. So his companion in the truth and the gospel, his fellow soldier Epaphras, was of Laodicea and was going back and forth, dealing with Laodicea directly.
precepts.point: Paul had a group of fellow soldiers that were about the work, not being pressured. They were about God's business.

note.label: Deceived by Enticing Words: Colossians 2

precepts.why:
Paul writes of the great conflict he has “for you, and for them at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh.” Laodicea is in Asia Minor. When you read the book of Acts, it is not written specifically that Paul went to Laodicea. He did go to Asia Minor, but it does not say he went to Laodicea. They had not seen his face in the flesh. One of his companions did go.

“Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. For I bear him record, that he hath a great zeal for you, and them that are in Laodicea, and them in Hierapolis.” His companion in the truth and the gospel, his fellow soldier Epaphras, was of that region, going back and forth, and he was the one dealing with Laodicea directly.

On the map of Asia Minor you see Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Smyrna, Philadelphia, Ephesus and Laodicea, with a river that splits between Ephesus, Philadelphia and Laodicea. Paul had a group of fellow soldiers like Epaphras who were about the work without being pressured. They were about God’s business, labouring fervently in prayer that the brethren would stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.

precepts.text: Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving. Watch and pray for your household, because if the house fails the nation gets weaker; it is not good for man to be alone.
precepts.point: Take ye heed, watch and pray, for ye know not when the time is. Stay ready.

note.label: Prepare Ye War

precepts.why:
Watching and praying is not only for the nation at large. “Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving”. Watch and pray for your household, your children, your brothers and sisters, because if the house fails, the nation gets weaker.

That is why marriage classes keep coming up. The scripture says it is not good for man to be alone. Some brothers think they are strong enough to do it without her, but it is not good that you should be alone; two are better than one.

And watch in the same with thanksgiving: be thankful for the things you have right now, because some people are in a way worse position than you. So continue in prayer, be thankful, and keep preparing, because you do not know when the time is.

precepts.text: Paul knew Luke personally and calls him the beloved physician, showing Luke was present throughout the ministry.
precepts.point: Theophilus' name means love of God. He was an Israelite, not a gentile, and Luke addresses him as "most excellent," a title of nobility or government office, the same way Paul addressed "most noble Festus."

note.label: Acts 1: The Promise of the Father and the Kingdom Restored to Israel

precepts.why:
“Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas, greet you.”

Paul knew Luke personally and calls him the beloved physician. That shows Luke was present throughout the ministry. He was not one of the twelve, but he was there, and what he wrote of “all that Jesus began both to do and teach” was delivered to him by eyewitnesses and written by a man who walked with the apostles.

note.label: Bishop Nathanyel | Revelation 3 A Message to The 7 Churches

precepts.why:
You can read about the church of Laodicea here. “For I bear him record, that he hath a great zeal for you,” talking about Epaphras, “and them that are in Laodicea, and them in Hierapolis. Luke, the beloved physician,” Luke was a doctor. “and Demas, greet you. Salute the brethren which are in Laodicea,” Salute the brothers that are in Laodicea. This is Paul writing about one of the seven churches. “and Nymphas, and the church which is in his house.” Nymphas had a church in his house.

“And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea.” You see that: so there was back and forth with letters to the church of Laodicea. Paul was checking up on them, making sure they were following the gospel.
